chunks.content: Effect of Nursing Interventions in Prevention and Healing of Incontinence-Associated Dermatitis among Critical Care Patients Jothi Clara J Micheal1, Merlyn Chander2, Jacintha D’Cruz3, Vevila Braganza4, Vinita Mascarenhas5, Pearl Cruz6 Abstract Incontinence is a common problem among hospitalised patients and has been associated with multiple health complications, including incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD) and hospital- acquired pressure ulcers (HAPUs). IAD is one of the clinical manifestations of moisture- associ- ated skin damage (MASD). IAD is a common problem in aged patients with faecal and/or urinary incontinence. In this study it was sought to reduce the incidence of IAD among critically ill patients admitted in ICU from 5.94 rate to <2.00 by implementing Nursing Interventions of IAD protocol. A one group pre-test post-test design was selected using consecutive sampling technique. The data was obtained by using an audit checklist prior and post-interventions. Results showed that the compliance to IAD protocol increased from 37.94 percent to 77.33 percent. Incidence of IAD reduced from 5.94 to 2.02 in the last 3 months. Healing status of IAD was 100 percent in June & July 2017. Thus nursing interventions are effective in the prevention and healing of IAD among critical care patients. documents.title: World Council of Enterostomal Therapists International Ostomy Guidelines

chunks.content: In rectal anterior resection, a temporary diverting loop ileostomy (DLI) is commonly performed for patients at high risk of anastomotic leakage. However, complications are more common in ileostomies than colostomies. Contributing factors include the thinner, more alkaline effluent from the small intestine, the difficulty of pouch adhesion when the stoma is flush or sunken, and the risk of dehydration and electrolyte aberrancies due to high output. , With the development of minimally invasive surgery and the pursuit of smaller incisions, laparoscopic techniques have been widely used in colorectal surgery. In laparoscopic anterior rectal resection (LAR), however, an auxiliary incision is still required for specimen extraction. To achieve incision-free surgery and more minimally invasive surgery, NOSES (natural orifice specimen extraction surgery) and its various modifications have been developed. – For patients scheduled for DLI in LAR, to avoid an additional auxiliary incision and achieve a more minimally invasive outcome, the specimen can be extracted through the enlarged stoma incision. – Postoperatively, the absence of auxiliary incisions promotes better recovery and improves postoperative aesthetics. In addition, specimen extraction through stoma incision (EXSI) is applicable in laparoscopic single-port surgery, as the single-port incision can be used for both specimen removal and stoma formation. However, EXSI surgery is associated with considerable stoma complications. – The EXSI technique requires extending the stoma incision by 6 to 10 cm to facilitate specimen extraction, which is excessively large for a typical ileostomy. The traditional suture method (TSM) reduces the incision to 3 cm by using interrupted sutures at both ends, leading to peristomal incisions. Due to the close proximity of this incision to the stoma, the highly corrosive intestinal fluid may cause incisional infection and secondary stomal complications. In our previous retrospective study, the reported stoma complication rate was 35.7% in LAR with EXSI surgery. To eliminate peristomal incisions and reduce skin infections, we proposed a novel stoma suturing technique that uses a skin-folding suture to reduce the enlarged incision size; it is named the “dumpling suture method (DSM)” due to its resemblance to the way Chinese soup dumplings are made with folds. In our previous retrospective cohort study, DSM was effective in protecting peristomal skin and significantly reduced the rate of stomal complications compared to the TSM. However, due to the retrospective nature of the study, the presence of multiple confounding factors attenuated the reliability of the conclusions, limiting the wider application of the DSM technique. To obtain higher-level evidence-based validation, we designed a single-center, prospective, open-label, randomized controlled study enrolling 72 patients who underwent LAR with EXSI surgery to determine whether DSM reduces stomal complications compared with TSM. MATERIALS AND METHODS Study Design and Participants This clinical trial was conducted as a single-center, randomized, open-label, 2-arm, parallel-group controlled study with equal allocation between the 2 arms. The trial began March 21, 2023, and concluded on December 6, 2024. Thirty-six patients were randomly assigned to the DSM group and 36 to the TSM group (Fig. ). The major eligibility criteria included the following: patients scheduled for LAR surgery with DLI and EXSI; no serious systemic infection or immunosuppression; aged between 18 and 100 years; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group Performance status of 0 or 1; expected survival time >6 months; and the patient participates voluntarily and signs an informed consent form. The exclusion criteria included any skin infectious disease in the abdominal wall, undergoing surgery <1 month since the last chemotherapy, having previously undergone any other stoma surgery, and the presence of a serious active infection requiring systemic therapy. During the study period, patients fulfilling the predefined inclusion criteria were consecutively recruited and underwent EXSI with either DSM or TSM procedures. This trial was conducted in full conformance with the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials guidelines. The study was approved by the hospital ethics committee (XHEC-C-2023-022-2). All patients provided written informed consent before enrollment. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT05985499 ). End Points and Questionnaires The primary end point was the rate of stoma-related complications within 1 month after surgery, defined as the occurrence of any of the following 7 conditions: fecal dermatitis, incision erosion/infection, mucocutaneous detachment, stomal hernia, stomal prolapse, stomal retraction, or stomal stenosis. Patients were considered to have a stoma-related complication if any 1 of these events occurred. The diagnostic criteria for each stoma-related complication were established with reference to the World Council of Enterostomal Therapists international ostomy guidelines (see Supplemental Table 1 at https://links.lww.com/DCR/C564 ). , The secondary end point was to investigate peristomal skin lesions, stomal pain score, and quality-of-life score within 1 month after surgery. Safety analysis was performed on the basis of early postoperative outcomes in the per-protocol (PP) population. The discoloration, erosion, and tissue overgrowth (DET) scoring system is a valuable tool specifically created for assessing the condition of peristomal skin lesions and is categorized into 4

any 1 of these events occurred. The diagnostic criteria for each stoma-related complication were established with reference to the World Council of Enterostomal Therapists international ostomy guidelines (see Supplemental Table 1 at https://links.lww.com/DCR/C564 ). , The secondary end point was to investigate peristomal skin lesions, stomal pain score, and quality-of-life score within 1 month after surgery. Safety analysis was performed on the basis of early postoperative outcomes in the per-protocol (PP) population. The discoloration, erosion, and tissue overgrowth (DET) scoring system is a valuable tool specifically created for assessing the condition of peristomal skin lesions and is categorized into 4 ordinal levels. The Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) was used to assess stoma-related pain, with patients rating their pain on a 0 to 10 scale under the guidance of enterostomal therapists. The quality of life of patients was evaluated using the City of Hope Quality of Life-Ostomy Questionnaire, a tailored instrument for individuals with ostomies. Patients rated how the ostomy affected their physical, psychological, and social well-being. The scale has a maximum score of 430, with higher scores reflecting a greater negative impact on the patient’s quality of life. Follow-up assessments were conducted by enterostomal therapists on postoperative days 1, 3, 7, 15, 30, and 90. The DET and NRS scores were obtained at each follow-up, and the highest values within 30 days after surgery were used for analysis. The quality-of-life evaluation was performed once at 30 days postoperatively. Postoperative recovery outcomes and general postoperative complications were recorded during the hospitalization period. Surgical Procedures Laparoscopic anterior rectal resection One day before surgery, all enrolled patients had their stoma positioned by the same enterostomal therapist. The surgery was performed according to the steps of anterior rectal resection. After transecting the rectum using a laparoscopic stapler, a 6 to 10 cm incision was made at the preoperatively localized stoma point. A wound protector was inserted at the incision, and the rectal specimen was extracted through the incision. The colon was dissected proximally to the tumor, and the rectal tumor was removed intact. A circular stapler nail seat was placed at the end of the descending colon, and pneumoperitoneum was reestablished, followed by an end-to-end anastomosis. To reduce the risk of parastomal hernia, before exteriorizing the ileum, the enlarged fascial defect was narrowed using interrupted 3-0 absorbable sutures to close the peritoneum and posterior sheath, followed by suturing of the anterior sheath, thereby reducing the fascial defect size to 3 to 4 cm. Dumpling suture method EXSI extends the stoma incision to 6 to 10 cm, whereas the DSM technique gradually reduces it by pleating the skin edges and fixing the stoma to the abdominal wall. DSM for ileostomy was as follows (Fig. ; see video at http://links.lww.com/DCR/C584 ): 1) the looped ileum was extracted through the incision, with a rubber ring inserted in the mesentery to prevent stoma retraction (removed 1–2 weeks postoperatively); 2) a 3-0 absorbable suture was threaded in a skin–ileum–skin sequence (U-shaped suture), maintaining a 3 to 4 mm distance between the 2 skin points; 3) for knotting, we used toothed forceps to lift the skin edges of the incision between the 2 points, pulled in a lateral direction, and knotted in the medial direction of the forceps; each knot forms a small skin-fold elevation; 4) approximately 8 to 12 sutures were placed to gradually reduce the skin defect to about 3 cm in diameter (approximately 2-finger in width), allowing the ileal limb to pass smoothly without obstruction. In cases with a thickened mesentery or bowel wall, the final skin aperture was slightly enlarged; 5) An incision was made at the top of the stoma. The stoma mucosa will naturally evert within 2 weeks postoperatively. Traditional suture method TSM for ileostomy was as follows: 1) the stoma incision was 6 to 10 cm in length, and both ends of the skin incision were closed intermittently with 3-0 absorbable sutures, thereby reducing the incision size to 3 cm (approximately 2 fingers in width); 2) The terminal ileum was pulled out in a loop through the abdominal incision with a rubber ring to prevent stoma retraction; 3) the stoma was fixed to the skin using interrupted sutures; and 4) an incision was made at the top of the stoma. After using the TSM, 2 sutured incisions were present adjacent to the stoma postoperatively (Fig. B). Randomization After the patients had completed all baseline assessments and provided written consent to be enrolled in the trial, they were randomly assigned (1:1) to the DSM or TSM group using a computer-generated list of random numbers with a simple randomization method. Random allocation was performed by a staff member with no clinical involvement in the study. The patients were enrolled and allocated by the enrolling doctors who were unaware of the randomization sequence. Blinding was not

made at the top of the stoma. After using the TSM, 2 sutured incisions were present adjacent to the stoma postoperatively (Fig. B). Randomization After the patients had completed all baseline assessments and provided written consent to be enrolled in the trial, they were randomly assigned (1:1) to the DSM or TSM group using a computer-generated list of random numbers with a simple randomization method. Random allocation was performed by a staff member with no clinical involvement in the study. The patients were enrolled and allocated by the enrolling doctors who were unaware of the randomization sequence. Blinding was not practically possible owing to the distinct stoma appearance between groups. Sample Size Calculations The PASS 15 software was used in a superiority design with a 5% significance level and 80% power, and the primary end point was the stoma-related complication rate. Based on our previous study, it was hypothesized that the stoma-related complication rate was 10% in the test group and 35% in the control group. The minimum sample size per group was calculated to be 32 cases based on a 1:1 allocation. Assuming a dropout/loss to follow-up rate of 10%, our final sample size was 72 patients. Statistical Analysis The primary and secondary end point analyses were based on the intent-to-treat (ITT) set. Safety analysis was based on the PP set. The Student t test and the Mann-Whitney U test were applied to analyze quantitative variables with normal and nonnormal distributions, respectively. Nominal variables were evaluated using Pearson’s χ 2 test and Fisher exact test. A multivariable logistic regression model was used to assess the risk of stoma-related complications, adjusting for covariates identified a priori (sex, age, BMI, diabetes, ASA classification, hemoglobin level, albumin level, current smoker status, and type of surgery) as clinically relevant. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS version 27 software. RESULTS Baseline Clinical Characteristics Eighty-four patients were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 7 did not met the inclusion criteria and 5 declined to participate preoperatively. A total of 72 patients were enrolled in the study, with 36 randomly assigned to the DSM arm and 36 to the TSM arm. Five patients did not undergo the planned DSM or TSM procedures due to intraoperative findings (2 converted to open surgery; 3 did not undergo stoma creation), and no patients were lost to follow-up after surgery. The primary and secondary end point analyses were based on the ITT data set. The safety analysis was based on the PP set (Fig. ). The 2 groups were well balanced with respect to demographic and clinical characteristics (Table ). Of the 72 patients, 65 (90.3%) were diagnosed with rectal cancer, 3 (4.2%) with ulcerative colitis, and 4 (5.5%) with familial adenomatous polyposis. The surgical approach did not differ between the 2 groups ( p = 0.252). Fifty-three patients (73.6%) underwent laparoscopic surgery, 13 (18.1%) underwent robotic surgery, and 4 (5.6%) underwent laparoscopic single-port surgery. All surgical specimens were removed through the stoma incision; thus, no additional auxiliary incisions were made on the abdominal wall. Early Postoperative Outcomes of Surgery The mean operative time of stoma suturing was comparable between the DSM group (10.6 min) and the TSM group (10.5 min; Table ). There were no significant differences in postoperative recovery times between the 2 groups, including the time to first flatus (DSM 2.0 vs TSM 2.3 days), first defecation (DSM 2.8 vs TSM 3.2 days), first meal (DSM 3.1 vs TSM 3.6 days), and postoperative hospital stay (DSM 9.1 vs TSM 10.4 days). In addition, we evaluated the postoperative complications potentially associated with a stoma in both groups and found no significant differences in postoperative intestinal obstruction ( p = 0.673), anastomotic leakage ( p = 1.0), or renal insufficiency ( p = 0.356). Stoma-Related Complications Within 1 Month After Surgery A representative well-healed stoma from the DSM group 1 month after surgery is shown in Figure A, with no evidence of skin folds or infection. When comparing the DSM and TSM groups regarding total stoma-related complications, a statistically significant difference was found. The total stoma-related complication rate was 11.1% and 41.7% in the experimental and control arm, respectively, with a significant difference ( p = 0.003; Fig. A; Table ). Compared with the TSM group, the DSM group had an unadjusted OR of 0.175 (95% CI, 0.051–0.6) for the risk of total stoma-related complications. Analysis of each type of stoma complication revealed that the advantage of DSM lies in the protection of peristomal skin. Compared to TSM, DSM significantly decreased skin-related stoma complications, such as fecal dermatitis (DSM 8.3% vs TSM 33.3%, p = 0.009), skin erosion or infection (DSM 0% vs TSM 25%, p = 0.002), and mucocutaneous detachment (DSM 2.8% vs TSM 13.9%, p = 0.199; Fig. ; Table ). In addition, DET scores were markedly

Analysis of each type of stoma complication revealed that the advantage of DSM lies in the protection of peristomal skin. Compared to TSM, DSM significantly decreased skin-related stoma complications, such as fecal dermatitis (DSM 8.3% vs TSM 33.3%, p = 0.009), skin erosion or infection (DSM 0% vs TSM 25%, p = 0.002), and mucocutaneous detachment (DSM 2.8% vs TSM 13.9%, p = 0.199; Fig. ; Table ). In addition, DET scores were markedly lower in the DSM group (Fig. B; Table ). However, other stoma-related complications, including stomal hernia, prolapse, retraction, and stenosis, showed no significant difference between the 2 groups. Skin-related stoma complications can lead to increased stoma pain, which in turn impacts the quality of life of patients. As shown in Figure C and Table , the NRS pain scores in the DSM group were significantly lower than those in the TSM group ( p = 0.004). Quality-of-life scores measured using the City of Hope Quality of Life-Ostomy Questionnaire were also assessed; patients in the DSM group exhibited improved quality of life compared to those in the TSM group (DSM 141.2 vs TSM 177.5, p = 0.001; Fig. D; Table ). Multivariate Analysis of Stoma-Related Complications A multivariate logistic regression model was applied to analyze the factors related to stoma-associated complications. The model incorporated variables that might influence stomal complications, including age, sex, ASA classification, BMI, diabetes, hemoglobin level, albumin level, and suture methods. Multivariate analysis revealed that the suturing method was the only risk factor for stoma-related complications (Fig. ). The adjusted OR for stoma-related complications in the DSM group was 0.17 (95% CI, 0.04–0.64; p = 0.009), indicating an independent protective effect of the DSM technique. DISCUSSION In an effort to reduce stoma-related skin infections and further refine minimally invasive surgery without auxiliary incisions, we introduced a novel stoma suturing technique, which we have named the dumpling suture method owing to its resemblance to the process of making Chinese soup dumplings (Fig. ). The DSM uses a skin-fold approach to gradually reduce the incision. This surgical approach eliminates the peristomal incisions, thereby reducing the risk of skin infections. Postoperatively, although several small folds are present around the stoma, they do not affect the tight adhesion of the stoma bag baseplate to the skin. Within 1 month after the DSM surgery, the folded skin healed and flattened, establishing a tight connection to the stoma. In our prior retrospective cohort study, we reviewed data from 29 patients with rectal cancer who underwent DSM surgery. The retrospective analysis revealed that the DSM group showed a lower stomal complication rate than the TSM group. To further confirm this finding, we designed the present prospective randomized controlled trial to provide higher-level, evidence-based validation for the broader application of the DSM. The primary and secondary end point analyses were based on the ITT set. The DSM group demonstrated a significantly lower overall stoma-related complication rate of 11.1%, compared to 41.7% in the TSM group. Multivariate regression analysis identified DSM as an independent protective factor for stomal complications. The reduction in stomal complications by DSM was primarily attributed to its protective effect on peristomal skin, as DSM secured the stoma tightly to the abdominal wall, avoiding peristomal incisions and thus preventing the risk of skin infections. DSM demonstrated a marked superiority in preventing skin-related complications, including fecal dermatitis, skin infections, and mucocutaneous detachment. The primary reason for the high incidence of dermatitis in the TSM group was poor adhesion of the stomal pouch. First, the adjacent incisions were highly susceptible to exposure to corrosive effluent, leading to local infection and uneven skin contour, which interfered with secure pouch attachment. Second, suturing of the peristomal incision often caused local skin irregularities, further hindering effective adhesion of the ostomy appliance in home-based stoma care settings. These factors collectively contributed to effluent leakage and skin irritation. Furthermore, the DET scoring was used to quantify peristomal skin-related stomal complications, with results showing that DSM significantly reduced DET scores. DSM also improved stoma-related pain scores and quality of life, likely owing to its protective role in peristomal skin and its reduction in stomal complications. In addition, this study compared the early postoperative outcomes between the 2 groups and conducted a safety analysis. No significant differences were observed in postoperative time to first flatus, first defecation, first meal, hospital stays, or postoperative complications, supporting the safety and feasibility of DSM. No significant differences were observed in postoperative time to first flatus, first defecation, first meal, hospital stays, or postoperative complications, supporting the safety and feasibility of DSM. In this study, DSM was not compared with the conventional DLI but rather with TSM as the control group. Both DSM and TSM are indicated for EXSI surgery and are not suitable for standard stoma surgery. In addition, DSM can also be applied in single-port laparoscopic surgery. For patients scheduled for a DLI, the single-port device can be placed in the lower right abdomen, allowing both specimen extraction and stoma formation, thus achieving a more minimally invasive surgical outcome (Fig. ). Notably, in EXSI procedures, the stoma incision is additionally extended, which may increase the risk of parastomal hernia. Therefore, before stoma suture, the peritoneum, posterior sheath, and anterior sheath should be sutured to reduce the fascial defect. In addition, to ensure consistency with the DSM group, an incision was made at the top of the stoma. The stoma mucosa will naturally evert within 2 weeks postoperatively (Fig. A). This stomal maturation technique does not increase the risk of peristomal infection or dermatitis and does not compromise the validity of skin infection assessment. The present study has some limitations. First, this study was conducted at a single center, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other institutions with different surgical practices. Second, due to the nature of the surgical technique used in this study, blinding was not feasible, which may introduce bias into the outcome assessment. Third, we have not evaluated the DSM technique in patients with BMI > 32, and this will be further investigated in future studies. For patients with severe obesity who are at risk for stoma tension, we recommend adjusting the stoma site to ensure it is constructed under low-tension conditions. Fourth, this study was designed to assess early postoperative outcomes within the first month after surgery. We recognize that the limited follow-up period does not allow for comprehensive evaluation of late-onset stoma-related complications, such as parastomal hernia. CONCLUSION The DSM technique uses a skin-folding suture to reduce the enlarged stomal incision, thereby decreasing stoma-related complications. This procedure offers a novel suturing approach for loop ileostomy with enlarged incision, effectively eliminating postoperative incisions and minimizing surgical trauma. Therefore, we recommend the routine application of the DSM technique for stoma suture in EXSI procedures. In addition, to broaden the application of EXSI surgery to larger patient populations, future clinical studies are needed to evaluate EXSI performed with DSM in comparison to the traditional extraction-site method. chunks.content: Policies and processes WCET® Journal adheres to the recommendations of the International Committee of Medical Journal Editors (ICMJE Recommendations) and is listed with the ICMJE accordingly. Editorial Board members may publish their research in the journal. WCET® Journal uses a double blind peer review process to ensure anonymity and remove any possibility of bias. The journal is provided to all members of WCET® as part of their membership. However, a Hybrid Open Access model exists with the WHAM Evidence Summaries for low- and middle- income countries, Editorials, News and views and reports being freely available. Authorship All authors must meet all four criteria for authorship as stated by the ICMJE definition of authorship. 1. Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis or interpretation of data for the work; AND 2. Drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content; AND 3. Final approval of the version to be published; AND 4. Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work in ensuring that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work are appropriately investigated and resolved. All authors and contributors (i.e., individuals who contributed to the preparation of the manuscript but who do not meet the ICMJE criteria for authorship, including medical writers/editors) must specify their individual contributions at the end of the text in the Acknowledgements section. Individuals who did not contribute to the manuscript development but who deserve to be acknowledged for their contribution to the study (e.g., study investigators, persons who provided important technical expertise, or the participants as a group) should be mentioned in the Acknowledgements section. Permissions If the author(s) wishes to reproduce copyrighted work, it is the responsibility of the author(s) to obtain written permission from the copyright holder and to submit the original copy of that permission to the editor. Acknowledgements Acknowledgements should be as brief as possible. Contributions from anyone who does not meet the criteria for authorship should be listed. For individuals thanked in this section, or acknowledged elsewhere in the text, please provide names (initials and surname) and affiliations. Any editorial assistance should be acknowledged. Conflict of interest The conflict of interest section in the manuscript submission process must be answered. It is the responsibility of all authors to disclose any financial and non-financial relationships that could be viewed as presenting a potential or actual conflict of interest. Conflicts of interest must be disclosed within the manuscript after the ethics statement. If this affects the anonymity of authors, it should be disclosed in the cover letter to the editor, or the title page, and not appear in the main document. If there are no conflicts of interest to report, this must be stated. Ethics statement Investigations in human and animal subjects must conform to accepted ethical standards. Authors must certify in the text that the research protocol was approved by a suitably constituted ethics committee of the institution within which the work was carried out and that it conforms to the WMA Declaration of Helsinki or a similar such statement from the author's country, such as the Statement on Human Experimentation or the Statement on Animal Experimentation by the NHMRC in Australia. In addition, study participants must provide informed consent and appropriate written consents and permissions. Releases must be obtained where authors wish to include any case details, personal information, and/or images of patients or other individuals. Participant consent must be documented in the text. Funding Sources of funding or acknowledgements of grant supports must be stated and the names of funding organisations should be written in full. If this affects the anonymity of authors, it should be disclosed in the cover letter to the editor, or the title page, and not appear in the main document. Where a funding source is declared, the role of the funding source (e.g., in-study design, data collection, analysis or interpretation of the data) must be described. If the funding source had no such involvement, this must be stated. Where no specific funding was received, please insert the following statement: ‘This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial or not-for-profit sectors’. Peer review WCET® Journal uses a double blind peer review process with manuscripts sent to at least two reviewers. Reviewers will score the manuscript and provide feedback to authors. Commonly, authors will be asked to revise their manuscripts at least once as a result of the peer review process. Data sharing WCET® Journal encourages all authors to lodge their manuscripts, and all supporting data that relate to them, in the repositories of the institutions in which they work/study/research. Furthermore, the manuscripts and supporting data should be made available as soon as possible wherever that can be achieved within the laws of copyright.

Corrections, retractions and expressions of concern The ICMJE recommendations for corrections and retractions and expressions of concern are followed by WCET® Journal. A corrigendum or an erratum will be published in the very next edition after the editor learns of a published error. If several and/or serious errors are found, a retraction will be considered and published. If doubt is raised as to honesty or integrity of a published article, an investigation by two editorial board members will be instigated which could lead to an expression of concern being published.
